content: AGG01 is the provisional designation for a newly identified antibiotic belonging to the Penicillin class. This compound was discovered in the breast milk of the Tammar Wallaby and has been reported to exhibit antimicrobial activity that is approximately one hundred times more potent than penicillin. AGG01 has demonstrated efficacy against a range of bacterial pathogens, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Escherichia coli (E. coli), Streptococci, Salmonella, Bacillus subtilis, Pseudomonas species, Proteus vulgaris, and Staphylococcus aureus. Although AGG01 has not yet been formally classified as a Beta-lactam antibiotic, it is identified as a cationic peptide. This type of molecule is a polycationic protein characterized by a high abundance of positively charged amino acid residues, specifically arginine and lysine. Structurally, AGG01 adopts an amphipathic conformation, meaning it possesses both hydrophobic (water-repelling) and hydrophilic (water-attracting) regions. This structural property enables AGG01 to interact with anionic lipids, such as phosphatidylglycerol, which are present in bacterial membranes. The mechanism of action of AGG01 involves its insertion into the bacterial membrane. It achieves this by competing with cross-linking proteins that stabilize the layers of the bacterial membrane. Once inserted, AGG01 forms transmembrane protein channels, which facilitate the transport of ions out of the bacterial cell. This ion efflux leads to significant osmotic imbalance, causing extensive leakage of essential intracellular molecules through these newly formed pores. The prevailing understanding is that this loss of critical cellular components ultimately results in bacterial cell death. Importantly, the bacterial membrane differs structurally from the plasma membrane of mammalian cells.
